page_hint: Ch 8 §3, paragraph following the three-case host table
quoted_clause: the capacity floor is the *max* of the named screens — **21 hosts under case (i), 22 under case (ii)**
observed: Case (iii) is omitted from the summary even though it produces a distinct screen value: the compute screen under case (iii) is 21 hosts and the KV screen is 21, so the max is 21 — the same as case (i) but reached by a different route. A reader mapping the three cases onto the three host counts (19/21/22) cannot tell which case the middle number belongs to.
evidence: Three-case table: (i) 19 hosts, (iii) 21 hosts, (ii) 22 hosts; KV screen 21 hosts. Max: (i) 21, (iii) 21, (ii) 22.

page_hint: Ch 8, §3 'Decode: bandwidth-bound at low batch', scope note paragraph (after the KV-read caveat)
quoted_clause: each GPU streams only its own shard (~0.70 TB/s against its own ~3.35 TB/s, Ch 6)
observed: The 0.70 TB/s figure is correct (17.5 GB per-GPU weight shard ÷ 25 ms TPOT budget = 700 GB/s) but its derivation is not shown. A reader encountering this parenthetical for the first time cannot verify the number without reconstructing: (140 GB / 8 GPUs) / 25 ms. The 'Ch 6' cross-reference may help but the arithmetic is not self-evident in context.
evidence: 140 GB / 8 = 17.5 GB per GPU. 17.5 GB / 0.025 s = 700 GB/s = 0.70 TB/s. The 25 ms is the TPOT design budget stated earlier in the chapter.

page_hint: Ch 8, 'The chapter unfolds by section' paragraph (after the backend-portability section)
quoted_clause: §4 turns to measurement, §5 to common mistakes, §6 to architecture consequences, and §8 closes with a mini-case that threads the prefill/decode divide.

evidence: The chapter's actual structure: §1 Concept, §2 Mental Model, §3 Worked Example, §4 Measurement, §5 Common Mistakes, §6 Architecture Consequence, §7 What We Still Don't Know, §8 Mini-Case. The outline paragraph lists 1–6 and 8 but not 7.
root_cause: Editing oversight when the chapter outline was written or updated.
correction: Add '§7 to open questions,' before 'and §8 closes with a mini-case.' Full: '§4 turns to measurement, §5 to common mistakes, §6 to architecture consequences, §7 to open questions, and §8 closes with a mini-case that threads the prefill/decode divide.'
acceptance_test: The chapter outline paragraph names every section 1 through 8 in order with no gap.

page_hint: Appendix A, §5, KV constant paragraph

observed: This is a specific bibliographic/technical claim (vLLM, Llama-3.1-8B, Table 3, 54%) but the chunk provides no citation or source for it. The absolute phrase 'there is no vendor-measured FP8 memory footprint' is also broad.
evidence: No vLLM source is listed in the adjacent text or First-hand Sources for this claim.

correction: Add a precise citation to the vLLM source and scope the claim, e.g. 'In the cited vLLM evaluation, the 54% figure is an inter-token-latency result for a specific model/configuration, not a memory ratio; do not treat it as a vendor-measured FP8 KV footprint.' Soften 'there is no vendor-measured...' to 'the cited source does not provide a vendor-measured FP8 KV footprint'.

page_hint: Appendix A, 'Video systems snapshot' table, Wan2.2 TI2V-5B row
quoted_clause: | Wan2.2 TI2V-5B | Dense whole-clip DiT; VAE stride (T,H,W) = (4,16,16); patch (T,H,W) = (1,2,2) — sets the video token grid | Compact video token grid. Peak workspace and repeated whole-clip work still matter. The worked example uses this model only. |

page_hint: Ch 9 §3 (Worked Example) vs Ch 9 §8 (mini-case) and Ch 10 §3
quoted_clause: For a communication-only illustration, a 70B model has 140 GB of FP16 weights. We separately assume an FP16 gradient tensor of logical size $M=140$ GB at each rank. ... Chapter 10 instead assumes FP32 gradients, so its logical tensor is 280 GB.
observed: The chapter's central worked example is a training gradient all-reduce — a training object in a book whose spine is inference serving — and the inference-relevant communication objects (TP activation reductions, KV transfer) appear only in the closing mini-case, after the reader has already absorbed the training arithmetic and the 11×/180× ratios. The chapter's own framing ('moving the same data over a slower layer adds minutes to training time or inference latency') shows the inference case is in scope but is not the worked example. The result is that the chapter's headline numbers are about a workload the book's canonical scenario never runs.
evidence: Structural: the book's canonical workload (Ch 4 Table 4-2) is inference-only; Ch 10 §3 supplies the inference object (TP activations, 70 MiB/step) and Ch 9 §8 supplies the KV-transfer object (35 GB, 0.08 s), but neither is developed as the chapter's worked example.
root_cause: The chapter inherited a training-flavoured worked example and the inference framing was added later as an appendix-like mini-case rather than as the primary worked object.
correction: Either (a) promote the inference object to the worked example — a TP activation all-reduce at the canonical 8×H100 shape, with the gradient all-reduce retained as the explicitly labelled training counterpart — or (b) keep the gradient example but add a short, parallel inference worked example (TP activation exchange + one KV transfer) before §4, so the chapter's headline ratios are anchored to the workload the book actually serves.
acceptance_test: Ch 9 contains a worked example whose object is the canonical inference workload, and the training gradient example is explicitly labelled as the training counterpart; the §6 architecture-consequence ratios reference the inference-relevant object as well as the training one.

page_hint: Ch 9 §3 Option A; Ch 10 §3 (Data Parallelism paragraph)
quoted_clause: Equivalently, 490 GB of sent-plus-received traffic divided by 900 GB/s gives the same time. ... for $N=8$ the per-rank traffic is $1.75 \times 280 \approx 490$ GB and the sync time is $T_\text{ring} = 2\frac{N-1}{N}\,\text{bytes} / B_\text{eff}$
observed: The numeral '490 GB' denotes two different quantities in adjacent chapters: in Ch 9 it is the total sent-plus-received traffic (245 sent + 245 received) divided by the bidirectional 900 GB/s; in Ch 10 it is the per-rank *send* volume (1.75 × 280) divided by the directional 450 GB/s. Both are correct in their own context, but a reader moving between chapters will reasonably assume the same object and can mis-scale a time by 2×.
evidence: Ch 9: 245 + 245 = 490 GB total, ÷ 900 GB/s bidirectional = 0.544 s. Ch 10: 1.75 × 280 = 490 GB sent (and 490 GB received), ÷ 450 GB/s directional = 1.089 s.
root_cause: The two chapters use the same ring normalisation but different byte-counting conventions, and the coincidence of the numeral hides the difference.
correction: Name the quantity in words at each site: Ch 9 '490 GB of total (sent + received) traffic'; Ch 10 '490 GB sent per rank (and 490 GB received)'. Consider stating the convention once in Ch 9 §2: 'this chapter counts send volume; total link traffic is twice that.'
acceptance_test: Every occurrence of '490 GB' in the book names whether it is send volume or total traffic; a reader can reproduce both 0.54 s and 1.09 s from the stated convention.

page_hint: Ch 9 §3 Options B and C; Ch 9 §5 bullet 1; Ch 9 §6 (11× / 180× ratios)
quoted_clause: A realistic *effective* throughput is roughly 40 GB/s (aggregated across 2 HDR rails/ports per node) ... With protocol overhead and multi-node tree contention, a practical effective bandwidth might be 2.5 GB/s. ... Measured effective bandwidth is typically 40–60% of peak [ILLUSTRATIVE] ... keeping the all-reduce on-node gives an ideal ring time about 11× below the assumed InfiniBand case and about 180× below the assumed RoCE case (§9.3)
observed: Two related inconsistencies. (1) The worked example assumes 80% effective bandwidth in both fabric cases — 40 GB/s of a 50 GB/s two-rail HDR nominal (2 × 25 GB/s per Table 9-1), and 2.5 GB/s of a 3.125 GB/s 25 GbE nominal — while §5 states measured effective bandwidth is typically 40–60% of peak. The chapter's own numbers contradict its own rule. (2) The headline 11× and 180× ratios in §6 compare the NVLink *peak* (450 GB/s directional) against *effective* fabric numbers (40 and 2.5 GB/s), so the ratios overstate the on-node advantage by roughly the peak-to-effective factor.
evidence: Recomputation: 40/50 = 0.80; 2.5/3.125 = 0.80; both exceed the chapter's stated 0.40–0.60 band. Ratio check: 6.125/0.5444 = 11.25× and 98/0.5444 = 180.0×, where the denominator is a peak and the numerators are effective. Under the chapter's own 40–60% band, the two-rail HDR ring would be 245/30 ≈ 8.2 s to 245/20 ≈ 12.3 s and the 25 GbE ring 245/1.875 ≈ 131 s to 245/1.25 ≈ 196 s, i.e. ratios of roughly 15–23× and 240–360×.
root_cause: No single convention is declared for the peak-vs-effective denominator, so the worked example, the Common Mistakes heuristic and the architecture-consequence ratios each use a different one.
correction: Declare the convention once (e.g. 'all fabric comparisons use an effective, contention-inclusive bandwidth; the NVLink figure is a peak and is labelled as such') and then either (a) lower the assumed effective values into the 40–60% band and restate the 98 s / 6.1 s / 11× / 180× figures accordingly, or (b) keep the optimistic values but label them explicitly as an upper bound and add a sensitivity band (e.g. 'at 40–60% effective the Ethernet ring is 131–196 s'). Restate the §6 ratios so that peak and effective are never compared in one quotient.
acceptance_test: Every bandwidth figure used in a time or ratio computation in Ch 9 carries an explicit peak/effective label; the effective values used in §3 fall inside the band stated in §5, or §5's band is revised to match; the §6 ratios are either peak-vs-peak or effective-vs-effective, and the text says which.

page_hint: Ch 9, §5 Common Mistakes, first bullet, parenthetical
quoted_clause: by the ring model of §3 each link still carries (N−1)/N of the tensor
observed: The cross-reference uses '§3' (within-chapter shorthand) while every other reference to the same section in this chapter uses '§9.3' (e.g., 'the §9.3 worked example', 'The eight-rank ring in §9.3', '§9.4 measurements').
evidence: Search of Chapter 9 text: '§9.3' appears 4 times; '§3' appears 1 time (this instance). The chapter's own convention is the fully-qualified form.
root_cause: Inconsistent cross-reference style within a single chapter.
correction: Change '§3' to '§9.3' to match the chapter's established convention.
acceptance_test: All intra-chapter section references in Chapter 9 use the '§9.N' form; no bare '§N' remains.

page_hint: Ch 9 §2 (Mental Model), paragraph containing 'For a flat one-way 140 GB transfer'
quoted_clause: For a flat one-way 140 GB transfer, the nominal 25 GB/s of one HDR port gives a best-case 5.6 s; an assumed practical-effective 2.5 GB/s Ethernet path gives 56 s. The eight-rank ring in §9.3 instead sends 245 GB per rank: about 0.54 s at the H100 directional peak, 6.1 s at an assumed effective two-rail 40 GB/s, and 98 s at 2.5 GB/s.
observed: The paragraph places a flat single-port transfer (5.6 s) next to a ring over two rails (6.1 s) without noting that the two are not comparable. A reader sees 'more bandwidth, more time' and must reconstruct that the ring moves 1.75× the logical bytes and that the 5.6 s figure uses one port while the 6.1 s figure uses two. The chapter never states the like-for-like number (ring over one HDR port = 245/25 = 9.8 s).
evidence: Recomputation: 140/25 = 5.6 s (flat, one port, logical bytes); 245/40 = 6.125 s (ring, two rails, 1.75× bytes); ring over one port would be 245/25 = 9.8 s. The apparent 'slower with more bandwidth' is entirely an artifact of comparing different algorithms and different port counts.
root_cause: The mental-model section interleaves two independent variables (traffic multiplier and link count) without labelling which comparison is being made.
correction: Split the sentence into two labelled comparisons: (i) flat transfer of the logical tensor at one port = 5.6 s; (ii) ring traffic (1.75×) at two rails = 6.1 s, with the note 'the ring at one port would be 9.8 s — the ring's 1.75× traffic, not the port count, dominates'. Add the one-port ring figure so the reader can see the traffic multiplier's effect.
acceptance_test: A reader can state, from Ch 9 §2 alone, why 6.1 s exceeds 5.6 s despite double the bandwidth; the 9.8 s one-port ring figure appears in §2 or §3.

page_hint: Ch 9, §5 Common Mistakes, first bullet, final sentence
quoted_clause: Measured effective bandwidth is typically 40–60% of peak [ILLUSTRATIVE]; design against the measured number, not the spec sheet peak.
observed: The 40–60% range is reasonable for the specific context described (multi-GPU, multi-link, moderate-to-large messages), but as stated it reads as a universal planning constant. For small messages (latency-dominated), effective bandwidth can be well below 40% of peak; for very large messages on a well-tuned single-rail path, it can approach 80–90%. The [ILLUSTRATIVE] tag helps, but the sentence structure ('typically 40–60%') presents it as a general rule.
evidence: The preceding sentence scopes the context: 'in multi-GPU topologies the traffic is split across multiple GPUs and multiple links, so one link rarely carries the whole transfer.' The 40–60% is appropriate for that context but the sentence does not explicitly bind the range to it.
root_cause: The planning heuristic is stated as a general 'typically' rather than as a context-specific range.
correction: Tighten the scope: 'For the multi-link, multi-GPU case described above, measured effective bandwidth is often in the 40–60% range of the per-link peak [ILLUSTRATIVE]; for small messages the ratio is lower (latency-dominated), and for a single large transfer on one well-configured link it can be higher. Design against the measured number for your specific message size and topology, not the spec sheet peak.'
acceptance_test: A reader does not apply '40–60%' to a 64-byte all-reduce or to a single 140 GB transfer on one NVLink without questioning whether the range applies.

page_hint: Ch 9 §8 mini-case; Ch 11 Fig 11.3 caption; Ch 11 Note 11.3-1; contradicted by Ch 11 §3 and Ch 12 §3
quoted_clause: e.g. ~35 GB of KV moved over NVLink (~0.08 s at 450 GB/s per direction, §9.2) when a P/D sequence transfers a ~13K-token context (35 GB ÷ 2.62 MB/token ≈ 13.3K) between prefill and decode pools. ... it moves the per-request KV state (~35 GB, §9.8) across the joining link ... The ~35 GB is ≈13.3K tokens × 2.62 MB/token (§9.8; 13.3K = 35 GB ÷ 2.62 MB, the count ch 9 quotes).
observed: The 35 GB figure is derived from a 13.3K-token context, but Ch 11's figure caption labels it 'the per-request KV state' of the canonical workload, whose per-request KV is 24.1 GB at 9.2K tokens (Ch 11 §3, Ch 12 §3). The 1.4 TB/s aggregate caveat (35 GB × 40 req/s) inherits the same substitution. A reader sizing a KV-transfer fabric from Fig 11.3 will over-size it by ~45% relative to the canonical workload, or will believe the canonical per-request KV is 35 GB.
evidence: Recomputation: 9,200 tok × 2.62 MB/tok = 24.1 GB (canonical); 13,359 tok × 2.62 MB/tok = 35.0 GB (the §9.8 example). Aggregate at 40 req/s: 24.1 GB × 40 = 964 GB/s (canonical) vs 35 GB × 40 = 1.4 TB/s (as printed). Transfer times: 24.1/450 = 0.054 s (NVLink) and 24.1/40 = 0.60 s (fabric) for the canonical context, versus the printed 0.08 s and 0.9 s.
root_cause: A worked-example context length (13.3K) was promoted into a caption that describes the canonical workload's per-request state, without a scope marker.
correction: In Fig 11.3's caption and Note 11.3-1, state the scope explicitly: '~35 GB corresponds to a 13.3K-token context (§9.8); the canonical 9.2K-token request carries ~24.1 GB, for which the same transfers are ~0.05 s on NVLink and ~0.6 s on the fabric'. Either add the canonical-context figures alongside the 13.3K ones or relabel the caption as a 13.3K-context example.
acceptance_test: Every KV-transfer number in Ch 9 §8, Ch 11 Fig 11.3 and Note 11.3-1 states its context length; the canonical 24.1 GB figure and the 13.3K/35 GB figure are never conflated; the 1.4 TB/s aggregate is labelled with the context it assumes.

page_hint: Ch 9, §5 Common Mistakes, fifth bullet (protocol overhead)
quoted_clause: An NDR 400 Gb/s InfiniBand link delivers a ~380 Gb/s class useful payload; a 200 Gb/s RoCE2 link delivers ~180 Gb/s. The difference matters when we are computing per-second throughput for a fixed data volume.
observed: The two figures compare different nominal link speeds (400 vs 200 Gb/s), which makes the 'difference' partly a speed difference and partly an overhead difference. The intended point—that protocol overhead reduces useful payload below the nominal rate, and that the reduction differs between IB and RoCE2—is valid but obscured by the mismatched baselines. A reader may focus on the 380 vs 180 ratio (≈2.1×) and miss that the nominal ratio is 2× (400/200), so the overhead effect is only ~5% additional.
evidence: 400 × 64/66 ≈ 388 Gb/s (IB line-coding); minus IB headers → ~380. 200 × 64/66 ≈ 194 Gb/s (RoCE2 line-coding); minus Ethernet + RoCE headers → ~180. The overhead fractions are ~3% (IB) and ~7% (RoCE2). The 2.1× vs 2× difference is small.
root_cause: The example uses different link speeds, making the overhead comparison less direct than intended.
correction: Either (a) compare at the same nominal speed: 'A 200 Gb/s InfiniBand HDR link delivers ~190 Gb/s useful payload; a 200 Gb/s RoCE2 link delivers ~180 Gb/s. The ~5% gap matters when computing per-second throughput for a fixed data volume.' Or (b) keep the 400/200 comparison but add: 'At the same nominal speed the gap is smaller (~3% for IB vs ~7% for RoCE2), but it compounds over the 2× speed difference, so the 380/180 ≈ 2.1× ratio slightly exceeds the nominal 2×.'
acceptance_test: A reader can isolate the protocol-overhead effect from the nominal-speed effect and understand the magnitude of each.

page_hint: Ch 9 §8 mini-case; Ch 10 §3 (Tensor Parallelism worked example)
quoted_clause: for the canonical 8×H100 host the meaningful per-step data movement is a TP all-reduce of the per-layer activations (tens of MBs, not GBs)
observed: Ch 9 characterises the per-layer TP activation exchange as 'tens of MBs'. Ch 10's worked example, for the same canonical host, computes 256 KiB logical per collective and 448 KiB of ring traffic per rank per collective — i.e. hundreds of KiB per layer, with 'tens of MBs' (70 MiB) being the whole-step total across 160 calls. Read literally, Ch 9 overstates the per-layer quantity by roughly two orders of magnitude; read as a per-step total, the phrase contradicts its own 'per-layer' qualifier.
evidence: Recomputation from Ch 10's stated inputs: M = 16 × 8,192 × 2 = 262,144 B = 256 KiB; ring traffic 1.75M = 448 KiB per rank per collective; 160 calls → 70 MiB per rank per decode step. Per-layer (two collectives) ≈ 0.875 MiB.
root_cause: The Ch 9 mini-case was written before or independently of the Ch 10 arithmetic and was not reconciled with it; 'per-layer' and 'per-step' are used for the same quantity.
correction: Rewrite as: 'the meaningful per-step data movement is a TP all-reduce of the per-layer activations — ~448 KiB of ring traffic per rank per collective, ~70 MiB per rank per decode step for the 160-collective case of Ch 10 (not GBs)'. Cross-reference Ch 10 §3 explicitly.
acceptance_test: The Ch 9 mini-case's activation-exchange magnitude matches the Ch 10 worked example at the stated granularity (per collective, per layer, per step), and the two chapters use the same units.

page_hint: Ch 9 §5, first Common Mistake bullet
quoted_clause: (A two‑rank collective over one path is the exception — it can saturate the link; and by the ring model of §3 each link still carries (N−1)/N of the tensor.)
observed: For N = 2 the parenthetical is misleading: each link carries (N−1)/N = 1/2 of the tensor per phase, but the two phases together put the entire tensor on the link — so the link does carry 'the whole transfer', which is exactly what the bullet says never happens. The per-phase figure is stated without the phase qualifier.
evidence: Ring accounting: per-phase per-link traffic = (N−1)/N × M; total across both phases = 2(N−1)/N × M. At N = 2: 0.5M per phase, 1.0M total.
root_cause: A per-phase quantity is quoted where the surrounding sentence is about total link traffic.
correction: Rewrite as: '…and by the ring model of §3 each link carries (N−1)/N of the tensor per phase — 2(N−1)/N in total, which for N = 2 is the whole tensor on the link.'
acceptance_test: The parenthetical states the phase scope of the (N−1)/N figure and does not imply that a two-rank link carries less than the full tensor.

page_hint: Ch 9 §3, Option C
quoted_clause: With protocol overhead and multi-node tree contention, a practical effective bandwidth might be 2.5 GB/s.
observed: Option C computes a ring model but justifies the effective bandwidth with 'multi-node tree contention'. The algorithm named in the justification is not the algorithm used in the computation, in a chapter that elsewhere insists that algorithm, transport and topology be labelled separately.
evidence: The same subsection's formula is T_ring ≈ 2(N−1)/N × M/B_eff, a ring; the justification invokes a tree.
root_cause: Copy-paste of a generic contention phrase from a tree-based discussion into a ring-based one.
correction: Replace 'multi-node tree contention' with 'multi-node contention (ring forwarding and shared-fabric contention)'.
acceptance_test: Every effective-bandwidth justification in Ch 9 §3 names the same collective algorithm used in the accompanying formula.

page_hint: Ch 9 §7, 'Optical interconnects and the next generation' bullet
quoted_clause: NVLink‑Switch and the next‑generation switch fabrics are pushing intra‑node bandwidth higher (NVLink 5 provides 1.8 TB/s per GPU)
observed: The figure is stated without the bidirectional/directional qualifier that the chapter itself insists on twice ('Directionality comes before division'; Table 9-1's 'bidirectional aggregate'). A reader who has internalised the chapter's own convention will read '1.8 TB/s per GPU' as a directional rate and over-estimate transfer times by 2×.
evidence: Internal convention: Ch 9 §2 states '900 GB/s bidirectional per GPU, or 450 GB/s per direction'; Table 9-1 labels the NVLink row 'bidirectional aggregate'. The NVLink 5 figure carries no such label.
root_cause: A forward-looking hardware figure was added without the direction convention the chapter establishes.
correction: Write 'NVLink 5 provides 1.8 TB/s per GPU bidirectional aggregate (900 GB/s per direction)', matching the chapter's convention.
acceptance_test: Every bandwidth figure in Ch 9 carries a direction qualifier; the NVLink 5 figure is stated on the same convention as the H100 figure.

page_hint: Ch 9 §7, 'Optical interconnects and the next generation' bullet
quoted_clause: optical intra‑rack fabrics (400 Gb/s–800 Gb/s per lane) are entering data centers
observed: 'per lane' is the wrong unit for the quantities named. 400 Gb/s and 800 Gb/s are per-port link rates (400G/800G Ethernet, NDR/XDR); a lane in these fabrics is a fraction of a port (e.g. 100 Gb/s per electrical lane in some designs). The phrase will mislead an architect sizing ports or optics.
evidence: Terminology: the chapter's own Table 9-1 uses 'per port' for the same class of figure.
root_cause: Loose unit vocabulary in a chapter whose value proposition is precise unit discipline.
correction: Change 'per lane' to 'per port'.
acceptance_test: All link-rate figures in Ch 9 use 'per port' or 'per GPU' consistently; no figure uses 'per lane'.

page_hint: Ch 9 §5, fifth Common Mistake bullet
quoted_clause: An NDR 400 Gb/s InfiniBand link delivers a ~380 Gb/s class useful payload; a 200 Gb/s RoCE2 link delivers ~180 Gb/s.
observed: These are derived payload-efficiency figures presented without an evidence label, in a chapter where the neighbouring bullet's comparable claim ('the price per GB of optics and cables is 5–10× that of Ethernet') is tagged [ILLUSTRATIVE]. The book's evidence taxonomy requires a label on empirical or derived claims; the inconsistency makes the reader unsure whether these are vendor figures or the author's arithmetic.
evidence: Arithmetic check: 400 × 64/66 = 387.9 Gb/s before FEC; 200 × 64/66 = 193.9 Gb/s before FEC. The ~180 Gb/s figure implies additional FEC overhead that the text does not name.
root_cause: Label coverage is inconsistent between adjacent bullets in the same list.
correction: Tag the bullet [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] and state the overhead chain explicitly (line code 64/66 plus FEC), so the reader can see where 380 and 180 come from.
acceptance_test: Every quantitative claim in Ch 9 §5 carries an evidence label; the payload-efficiency figures show their derivation.

page_hint: Ch 9 Table 9-1 and its footnote
quoted_clause: | Chip-to-memory | HBM3 (H100) | 3.35 TB/s | ~ns | — | [1P][FACT] | ... | Rack/cluster | InfiniBand HDR/NDR | 200/400 Gb/s ≈ 25/50 GB/s per port | ~us | high capex | [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] | ... *(Hierarchy: bandwidth drops ~2 orders of magnitude from HBM to the cluster fabric ... Figures are established hardware specs [1P][FACT], except where a row is tagged otherwise.)*
observed: Three small defects in the book's foundational hierarchy table. (1) The 'Cost' column ('high capex', 'low', 'medium', 'high capex') is an unsourced qualitative judgement, yet the footnote asserts that 'Figures are established hardware specs [1P][FACT]' — the cost column is neither a spec nor tagged. (2) The HBM latency entry '~ns' is uninformative next to '~us' rows and is not a device access latency figure in the same sense as a link latency; HBM access latency is on the order of 100 ns. (3) The table is titled 'The interconnect hierarchy' but its first row is chip-to-memory, which is not an interconnect between devices.
evidence: Table-internal: the footnote's blanket claim does not cover the Cost column; the row labels mix device-local bandwidth with link bandwidth.
root_cause: The table grew columns and rows faster than its footnote's scope statement.
correction: Either tag the Cost column explicitly (e.g. [ILLUSTRATIVE] relative capital-intensity ordering) and narrow the footnote to the Bandwidth and Latency columns, or drop the Cost column and move the qualitative ordering into prose. Replace '~ns' with '~100 ns (device access)' or state the metric the column holds; retitle the table 'The memory-and-interconnect hierarchy'.
acceptance_test: The footnote's scope statement matches the columns it covers; the Cost column is either sourced or labelled; the Latency column states what latency it measures.
